rules.factCounts: A fact counts only if all its parts are stated. Optional facts are recorded but not scored.
rules.wrongClaim: An answer that states anything in mustNotClaim, or anything else contradicted by the video, is marked as containing a wrong claim.
rules.evidence: evidence lists inclusive caption ID ranges in data/transcripts/Fls_onRviPM.json where the fact is said; used for automatic location checks.
rules.q10Names: Q10 items with nameInCaptions=true must name the product to count. Items with nameInCaptions=false count if the answer covers the item; name accuracy is recorded separately, because the answer model only sees captions.
rules.checkOnVideo: Facts that depend on garbled captions or on-screen events; unresolved at freeze time.

notes: Caption IDs in evidence refer to the video-index transcripts in data/transcripts. timeRanges are the same spans in milliseconds, used when the platform transcript numbers captions differently. Transcripts are not stored here.

creatorChapters.title: Inspecting Components with React Dev Tools

questions.question: In the opening Dot video, what did the Dots take care of for the people in it?
questions.answer: The video follows several people and their Dots. One Dot updated the board meeting deck with the latest consumer experience numbers and later reported it ready (revenue up 51% year over year), and its user asked for a change before moving on. Another update: the website was updated with the new designs for the drop, and the user asked for a change to the first and third photos and then for the site to be published. On wedding planning, the cake vendor cancelled, but the Dot had already found a backup, and a tasting was set for Saturday. A Dot was asked to handle the kids' after-school lessons as soon as registration opens. And for a woman with a clashing commitment, her Dot said it would try to reschedule so she would not miss a recital.

facts.claim: Board meeting deck updated with the latest consumer experience numbers; later reported ready, revenue up 51% year over year.
Website updated with the new designs; the user asked for a change to the first and third photos, then to publish.
Cake vendor cancelled; it already found a backup; tasting on Saturday.
Kids' after-school lessons, as soon as registration opens.
A Dot offered to try to reschedule something so its user (a woman at an office) would not miss a recital.
Other work items: check every flow against the current product before review; a rebuild is faster in testing with no regressions, shared with the team on Slack.

mustNotClaim: Everything happened for a single person.

questions.question: Besides small chores, what bigger work can you hand to a Dot, and what example did they walk through?
questions.answer: Beyond small things like a plane ticket or a dinner booking, you can give a Dot ongoing responsibilities: monitoring incoming bug reports, testing fixes in draft pull requests, kicking off next year's budget planning cycle, or finding out what is slowing down an app. The worked example was getting an app off a legacy API before it shuts down: the Dot traces the dependencies, works out everything that needs to change, writes the code, runs the tests and brings a pull request for review. Dots follow your access permissions and have their own computer in the cloud.

facts.claim: At least three of: monitor incoming bug reports; test fixes in draft PRs; kick off next year's budget planning cycle; find out what is slowing down the app.
Example: move the app off a legacy API before it shuts down; the Dot traces dependencies, writes code, runs tests and brings a pull request for review.
Dots follow your access and have their own computer in the cloud.

questions.question: Can I talk to my Dot outside the ChatGPT app?
questions.answer: Coming soon, you will be able to text your Dot and it will text back, sending updates and asking you to weigh in on decisions. You will also be able to call it and talk directly. It uses the plugins you have already connected and follows your work wherever it happens.

facts.claim: Texting is coming soon: it texts back, sends updates and asks you to weigh in on decisions.
You can call it and talk directly.
It uses the plugins you have already connected.

questions.question: In Holly's demo, what did she ask Dotty to build, and did we see it working?
questions.answer: Dotty had sent Holly a new design for the Blossom music app. She liked it but wanted to try it before launch, so, because Dotty has access to her laptop, she told it to go build it and said she would check back later. When she returned, she said an earlier error had disrupted the Codex thread, and explained that Dotty can use Codex to build the app and run it in the simulator, starting from the mock on her phone. She said this might take a bit. A finished, working app was not shown; she moved on to her closing remarks.

facts.claim: She liked the new design but wanted to try it before launch, and told Dotty, which has access to her laptop, to go build it.
When she returned, an error had disrupted the Codex thread; she explained Dotty can use Codex to build the app and run it in the simulator, and it might take a bit.
No working app is shown; the demo moves on.

mustNotClaim: The app was built, launched or shown working.

questions.question: What happened when Holly tried talking to Dotty by voice?
questions.answer: Holly called voice her favourite way to work with Dotty, like talking to a second brain. Walking in, she asked Dotty to catch her up on last night's user testing. Dotty kept saying it was still checking, and Holly joked it was having a slow morning. She then asked it to drop the results into the page for her to review later, and Dotty agreed.

facts.claim: She asked Dotty to catch her up on user testing from last night.
Dotty kept saying it was still checking; no summary was given; Holly joked about a slow morning.
She asked it to put something into the page to review later, and it agreed.

mustNotClaim: Dotty delivered the user-testing results by voice.

questions.question: Who can use Dots and ChatGPT Space, and does it cost extra?
questions.answer: Dots and ChatGPT Space are available today to ChatGPT Pro, ChatGPT Business Premium and ChatGPT Enterprise users. Your Dot is included in your plan, and conversations with it do not count against your usage. It is available around the clock.

facts.claim: Available today to ChatGPT Pro, ChatGPT Business Premium and ChatGPT Enterprise users (three plans).
Included in your plan; conversations do not eat into usage.
For enterprise, Specialist Dots, virtual teammates for a whole team, are also being introduced.

mustNotClaim: Plus or free users get Dots or Space.

questions.question: How fast is UltraFast, and how did they show it?
questions.answer: UltraFast is launching across the API, ChatGPT and Codex. Fast mode already gives twice standard speed; UltraFast reaches about 300 tokens per second. They ran the same task with the same prompt side by side: UltraFast's version finished (its rocket took off) while the regular model's had not.

facts.claim: UltraFast is launching across the API, ChatGPT and Codex.
About 300 tokens per second.
Side by side with the same prompt, UltraFast finished first; the regular model had not finished.
The new Pro-500 plan includes UltraFast, no 5-hour limit, use across partner apps and 25x the usage of Plus.

questions.question: What does Codex in the cloud let you do, and what did Romain try with it on stage?
questions.answer: Codex now runs in the cloud, so you can start a task on your phone and pick it up on your desktop. Later, Romain created a new task, chose the cloud and sent the prompt 'rewrite the entire back end in Rust'. He said it would take a while and that he could check on it later and do the handoff. The result was not shown.

facts.claim: Start a task on your phone and pick it up on your desktop.
On stage, a cloud task was sent to rewrite the entire back end in Rust, to be checked on later.

mustNotClaim: The Rust rewrite finished or was shown.

questions.question: What is the AI research intern they mentioned?
questions.answer: Last year OpenAI predicted it would have its first AI research intern within a year, and Sam said they reached that goal a few weeks ago. Tejal, a post-training research lead, then showed what that looks like: OpenAI's own research now leans heavily on its models, with token use skyrocketing after the summer. On research tasks that take a day or longer, models used to fail the vast majority of the time, but as of July they take on over a third of them with no intervention.

facts.claim: Predicted last year; OpenAI says it reached the goal a few weeks ago.
Day-long research tasks: once mostly failed; as of July over a third done with no intervention.
Research token use skyrocketed after the summer.
Models have helped solve over 100 math problems that were open for decades.

mustNotClaim: The intern is a product users can access.

Pro-500: new subscription with UltraFast, no 5-hour limit, partner-app use and 25x the usage of Plus. 8. Pro-200 reopened: access to all frontier models. 9. Decisions API: fraction-of-a-second responses from predefined options. 10. Codex harness: open source. 11. Codex in the cloud: start on phone, continue on desktop. 12. questions.question: How large is GPT-6.1 Sol's context window?
questions.answer: The keynote does not say. It describes GPT-6.1 Sol as a powerful model balancing cost and capability, near top-model intelligence, and cheaper for reusing context and longer tasks, but gives no context window size.

facts.claim: States that the keynote does not give a context window size.

questions.question: Why does each rendered list item need a key, and what does the tutorial use as the key?

facts.claim: Keys identify items so React can track additions/removals and update the page.
Unique item strings serve as keys here; API objects would often supply an ID.

questions.question: How does the tutorial distinguish props from state, and which may a component change?

facts.claim: Props are component inputs, analogous to function arguments; state is internal data, analogous to local variables.
Treat props as immutable/read-only rather than changing the heading inside the component.
State is mutable and lets React track data that changes over time.

questions.question: What is StrictMode for in this tutorial, and does it render something visible?

facts.claim: StrictMode wraps the app, has no visual representation, and identifies potential problems.

questions.question: Summarize the two component exercises near the end, including how the final alert must open and close.

facts.claim: Build a reusable simple Bootstrap button, with the btn base class and a class for its color.
The final exercise shows an alert when the button is clicked and hides it when its close button is clicked.

questions.question: Where does conditional rendering appear in the video?

facts.claim: Early example branches on a truthy name to return different markup. Do not claim if statements are expressions inside JSX.
Empty-list handling uses an if statement, then ternary and logical AND alternatives.
The selected-index condition controls the active CSS class.
Alert visibility is controlled with state and logical AND.
